strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: generalizable Gaussian reconstruction from images containing transient distractors, without per-scene optimization.
Reference-guided correction of residual masks is well motivated: it can restore supervision on difficult static regions that conventional robust losses incorrectly suppress.

The reported improvements are substantial. DGGS-TR achieves 21.02 dB versus 19.29 dB for the strongest adapted masking baseline and 15.45 dB for retrained MVSplat; full DGGS reaches 21.74 dB. Table 2 provides useful component ablations, and outdoor-to-indoor transfer offers positive evidence of generalization.
weaknesses: The inference evaluation uses a favorable, curated reference-pool protocol. Section 5.1.2 explicitly ensures that pools contain some distractor-free images and selects candidates near the target view. This tests selection under favorable availability conditions but does not establish robustness for arbitrary adjacent views or entirely contaminated pools. Performance should be measured against clean-view availability and distractor severity.

Several central claims lack quantitative support. Superior mask accuracy over scene-specific methods is supported only by qualitative examples, without annotated-mask metrics. Synthetic Re10K/ACID results are also qualitative, and claims about training stability lack learning curves or repeated-run statistics.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the supplied manuscript. Training schedules, initialization, image resolution, baseline adaptation details, synthetic-data construction, and several mask-refinement settings are missing or deferred to an appendix that is absent from the supplied PDF. These omissions particularly hinder interpretation of the large gap between retrained and pretrained baselines.

The reference-selection comparisons do not isolate the proposed scoring mechanism sufficiently. Table 4 compares selecting four views against directly using eight, but lacks alternative four-view selectors operating on the same eight-image pool, such as segmentation-based cleanliness ranking or geometric coverage selection. It is consequently unclear how much improvement requires the proposed coarse reconstruction and mask scoring.

Important algorithmic details remain ambiguous, including visibility and depth-conflict handling during mask warping, the exact mask decoupling/recombination procedure, and the common-occlusion rule that disables pruning. Moreover, low reference reconstruction error need not imply a static region: an input-conditioned model can reproduce transient objects. The reliability of this central assumption is not directly evaluated.

The technical novelty is primarily a combination of established residual masking, entity segmentation, geometric warping, view selection, and Gaussian pruning. This potentially useful integration needs stronger experimental isolation and broader quantitative validation to establish a contribution competitive with a top-tier venue. The efficiency comparison also omits hardware and resolution and does not clearly separate reconstruction, segmentation, and rendering costs.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: feedforward Gaussian reconstruction from images containing transient distractors, including training on contaminated data and generalization to unseen scenes.

The reference-guided mask filtering provides a plausible way to recover static regions incorrectly excluded by residual-based masking. Table 2 supports its contribution, increasing mean PSNR from 17.11 to 20.35 dB.

Reported reconstruction improvements are substantial: DGGS-TR achieves 21.02 dB versus 19.29 dB for MVSplat+SLS, and the complete framework reaches 21.74 dB on five RobustNeRF scenes. Component ablations and qualitative examples support benefits from refinement, reference selection, and pruning.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not adequately establish robustness under unconstrained capture. Section 5.1.2 explicitly constructs candidate pools containing some distractor-free images, favoring the proposed selection mechanism. Results with naturally sampled pools, no clean references, and controlled distractor coverage are needed to support the broader deployment claims.

The claimed superiority in mask accuracy over scene-specific methods is supported only by selected qualitative examples in Figure 6. No mask IoU, precision, recall, or annotated evaluation is reported. Likewise, improved training stability is inferred from final reconstruction scores rather than convergence measurements or variability across runs.

Important reproduction details are absent from the supplied manuscript. It repeatedly refers to an appendix, but the provided PDF ends with references. Training schedules, initialization, image resolution, baseline adaptation details, synthetic-data construction, segmentation thresholds, and precise visibility handling and pruning rules are insufficiently specified.

Baseline controls leave important questions unresolved. Transferring scene-specific masking methods into MVSplat is reasonable, but their adaptation and tuning are not documented sufficiently to establish competitive implementations. Reference selection is compared with directly using eight references, but not with simpler selection strategies operating on the same eight-image pool, such as segmentation-based distractor ranking or pose-diverse selection.

Evidence for broad generalization is limited. The main quantitative feedforward evaluation covers five indoor scenes; the two outdoor scenes receive quantitative evaluation after scene-specific fine-tuning. Synthetic Re10K/ACID results are qualitative in the supplied document, and no repeated-run uncertainty is reported.

The technical contribution primarily combines existing robust residual masking, geometric warping, pretrained entity segmentation, reference ranking, and Gaussian removal. The reference-guided filtering is useful, but the paper does not sufficiently establish its reliability when transient objects are themselves reconstructed accurately in reference views or when depth and visibility estimates are wrong.

Efficiency claims are difficult to assess: Table 5 reports 'rendering time' without hardware, resolution, or a clear accounting of reconstruction, candidate scoring, segmentation, and rendering. The reported 0.148 seconds versus 0.084 seconds for MVSplat is approximately 76% overhead, making the characterization as a slight decrease insufficiently justified.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: feedforward reconstruction of unseen scenes containing transient distractors. Jointly addressing distractors during training and inference is a useful contribution.
The reference-based mask correction is well motivated: multi-view evidence can help distinguish difficult static regions from distractors that residual-based masking would otherwise conflate.

The reported reconstruction improvements are substantial. In Table 1, DGGS-TR achieves 21.02 dB versus 19.29 dB for MVSplat+SLS and 20.03 dB for pretrained MVSplat; the complete framework reaches 21.74 dB.

The component ablations provide meaningful evidence, particularly the improvement from 17.11 to 20.35 dB after adding reference-based mask prediction. Outdoor-to-indoor evaluation and the fine-tuning comparisons provide additional positive evidence.
weaknesses: The evaluation deliberately constructs reference pools containing some distractor-free images (Section 5.1.2), favoring the reference-selection mechanism. Performance with naturally sampled pools, entirely cluttered pools, and varying occlusion severity is not established. Comparing against eight unfiltered references does not replace comparisons with simpler selection strategies using the same candidate pool and compute budget.

The supplied manuscript repeatedly defers essential information to an appendix that is absent. Training schedules, initialization, image resolution, hardware, segmentation thresholds, synthetic-data construction, and detailed baseline adaptations are insufficiently specified. This materially limits reproducibility and confidence in the comparisons.

The central claim of mask accuracy exceeding scene-specific methods is supported only by selected visual examples. There are no quantitative mask metrics or annotated evaluation protocol. The breadth of quantitative generalization evidence is limited. The main reconstruction table reports a five-scene mean and only two individual scenes; synthetic Re10K/ACID results are qualitative. The outdoor quantitative results in Table 3 involve test-scene fine-tuning and therefore do not establish feedforward generalization on those scenes.

Important algorithmic details remain ambiguous. The final mask decoupling/recombination operation and the common-occlusion test controlling pruning are not explicitly defined. Equation 7 produces a coverage mask whose zeros denote uncovered regions, but its subsequent use is left informal. Warping visibility and depth-conflict handling also require clarification because they directly affect mask validity.

The reference-based correction is promising, but the missing implementation details and evaluation controls prevent the evidence from establishing a sufficiently strong advance for acceptance. strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: removing transient distractors during both training and feed-forward inference of generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting.

Reference-based mask correction is a useful contribution with substantial measured benefits. Table 2 improves PSNR from 17.11 with robust masking to 20.35 with reference-based prediction, and to 21.02 with refinement.

The evaluation includes comparisons with several adapted masking methods, outdoor-to-indoor transfer, synthetic distractors, and ablations of training, inference, and segmentation components. DGGS-TR outperforms the strongest retrained masking baseline in Table 1 by 1.73 dB.
The paper acknowledges persistent occlusion failures and reports the additional inference cost rather than presenting artifact removal as universally successful.
weaknesses: The inference evaluation uses a favorable reference-pool construction. Appendix A.2 explicitly ensures that candidate pools contain some distractor-free images, whereas deployment is claimed to work with arbitrary adjacent views. Cross-scene performance with exclusively cluttered pools and varying clean-image availability is not established. Table 13 compares against using all eight references, but does not compare scoring against simpler selection methods given the same candidate pool.

The prominent claim of mask accuracy exceeding scene-specific methods is supported only by qualitative examples. No mask IoU, precision, recall, or boundary metrics are reported, even though synthetic insertion provides ground-truth masks. Reconstruction improvements alone cannot establish superior distractor identification.

The baseline training setup leaves important confounds unresolved. Models are retrained for only 10,000 iterations on a small collection of scenes, and retrained MVSplat performs substantially worse than its pretrained counterpart. Initialization, optimization settings, and convergence are insufficiently documented to separate distractor robustness from training-budget and domain effects. The fine-tuning experiments in Table 3 are scene-specific and do not resolve this cross-scene comparison.

Several central implementation details are underspecified. Equation 6 unions warped all-one masks, which represents projected coverage, while the surrounding text describes regions absent from all references; the polarity and final mask recombination are unclear. Visibility handling during warping, segmentation filling thresholds, and the exact common-occlusion test controlling Gaussian pruning are also missing. These details materially affect the proposed method.

Generalization evidence remains limited: the full inference framework is quantitatively evaluated on a small indoor benchmark, while outdoor results omit it. Synthetic results compare mainly with pretrained MVSplat, without equally fine-tuned robust baselines, and omit dataset sizes and exact splits. Reported scene counts are also inconsistent between the dataset description and the five-scene averages. No uncertainty estimates are supplied.

The contribution combines established residual masking, segmentation refinement, geometric warping, reference selection, and pruning. The reference-based correction has demonstrated value, but broader integration is tested only with MVSplat, and the central assumption that accurate reference reconstruction identifies static content lacks direct quantitative validation. Together with the evaluation and reproducibility gaps, the evidence is insufficient for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: removing transient distractors during both training and inference of generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting. Using reference-view consistency to refine residual masks is a sensible contribution.

The reported reconstruction improvements are substantial under the proposed protocol. On the five-scene aggregate in Table 1, DGGS-TR achieves 21.02 dB versus 15.45 for retrained MVSplat and 19.29 for MVSplat+SLS; the complete inference framework increases this to 21.74 dB.

The paper includes useful component ablations, segmentation-model substitutions, synthetic experiments, and qualitative failure cases. Table 2 identifies reference-based mask prediction as the main source of improvement, while the segmentation ablations suggest that gains do not depend strongly on a particular segmentation model.
weaknesses: The inference evaluation favors the proposed selection mechanism in a way that limits the conclusions. Appendix A.2 explicitly constructs candidate pools near the target view and ensures that they include some distractor-free images. Performance with naturally sampled pools or no clean candidates is not established quantitatively. Table 13's comparison against feeding all eight references does not replace comparisons with simple pose-based, segmentation-based, or random four-of-eight selection under identical candidate pools.

The baseline evidence does not fully establish superiority under a strong, matched training protocol. Most primary comparisons involve models retrained for 10K iterations on a small collection of scenes, while pretrained MVSplat already reaches 20.03 dB. The adapted scene-specific methods are incomplete versions of their original systems—for example, NeRF-HuGS excludes Nerfacto. These adaptations are reasonable experimental baselines, but their limitations need clearer qualification and stronger comparisons using matched pretrained initialization and distractor-aware fine-tuning on held-out scenes.

The prominent claim that feed-forward masks outperform scene-specific distractor-removal methods is supported only by qualitative examples. No mask IoU, precision, recall, or boundary metrics are reported, even though synthetic compositing provides ground-truth distractor masks. Reference-view PSNR in Table 6 also does not establish that residuals reliably distinguish static regions from distractors.

The evaluation is too limited and insufficiently specified for the breadth of the generalization claims. Reconstruction experiments primarily use 192×256 images and a small real-scene collection. Synthetic training/test set sizes and exact splits are missing, and Table 10 compares only against pretrained MVSplat rather than the stronger adapted baselines. The description of four RobustNeRF scenes versus the reported five-scene aggregate also needs reconciliation. No variability across runs or uncertainty estimates is provided.

Important implementation details remain ambiguous. The exact decoupling and recombination producing the final mask M are not formalized, the segmentation filling threshold is unspecified, and the visibility handling and common-occlusion exception used in Gaussian pruning lack a reproducible algorithm. Training initialization, optimizer settings, and the synthetic dataset manifest are also insufficiently documented; code is only promised upon publication.

The technical advance is primarily an integration of existing residual masking, segmentation refinement, geometric warping, reference selection, and pruning. The reference-based filter has encouraging ablation evidence, but the claimed applicability across generalizable 3DGS frameworks is demonstrated only on MVSplat. Together with the unresolved evaluation issues, this leaves insufficient evidence of a contribution competitive with the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: training and deploying generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting with transient distractors. The reference-based masking approach is a meaningful adaptation beyond directly transferring scene-specific robust losses.

Reports substantial improvements under matched training conditions. DGGS-TR achieves 21.02 dB versus 15.45 for MVSplat and 19.29 for MVSplat+SLS; the complete inference framework improves this to 21.74 dB.

Component ablations provide concrete evidence for the method: reference-based masking raises PSNR from 17.11 to 20.35, with further gains from refinement, reference scoring, and pruning. Additional segmentation and mask-fusion experiments strengthen the analysis.

Outdoor-to-indoor evaluation, synthetic examples, and scene-specific fine-tuning provide complementary evidence. Qualitative results demonstrate reduced artifacts, and the paper acknowledges failure under persistent occlusion.
weaknesses: The inference evaluation uses a favorable reference-pool construction: Appendix A.2 explicitly ensures that nearby candidate views include some distractor-free images. Performance with naturally sampled pools, entirely cluttered references, and increasing persistent occlusion is not systematically quantified. Comparing against eight unselected references does not replace simple selection baselines operating on the same candidate pool.

The prominent claim that feed-forward masks outperform scene-specific methods is supported by qualitative examples rather than quantitative segmentation evaluation. Mask IoU, precision, and recall—particularly on synthetic data with available distractor masks—are needed. Higher reference re-rendering PSNR alone also does not establish that low residuals reliably distinguish static content from distractors.

Generalization evidence remains limited. Experiments primarily use one backbone and low-resolution images, while the synthetic dataset lacks explicit scene counts and reproducible splits. Table 10 compares DGGS against pretrained MVSplat without matched synthetic fine-tuning or robust-loss baselines, weakening attribution of the large gains.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the stated commitment to release code. Training initialization, optimizer settings, segmentation-fill thresholds, visibility handling during warping, and the precise common-occlusion pruning rule need clearer specification. The description of four RobustNeRF scenes also needs reconciliation with the five-scene averages in the tables.

The contribution combines established robust masking, segmentation refinement, view selection, and Gaussian pruning. The reference-based component has persuasive ablation support, but the broader novelty and superiority claims exceed the current evaluation. Overall, this is promising work with meaningful measured gains, but the protocol limitations and unsupported mask-accuracy claim place it slightly below the acceptance threshold.
